newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock experts applaud IMF's cautionary comments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock experts applaud IMF's cautionary comments.

text.p: International Monetary Fund comments about the "rich" nature of U.S. stock prices were welcomed by stock analysts, who said Thursday that market excesses persisted and needed to be curbed.
A near-10 percent correction in the Dow industrials in March and early April convinced many experts that investors have already become more rational and less exuberant.
Nevertheless, they said market caution is still warranted and that this week's IMF rhetoric has helped highlight the need for investors to remain selective.
After undergoing a 9.8 percent correction between March 11 and April 11, the Dow industrials have regained nearly two-thirds of that lost ground.

"I think it's brave and appropriate for these officials to speak out," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "We still have excesses and if enthusiasm is unbridled, the negative impact of a downturn could be dramatic."
On Thursday, IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus seconded remarks made by his chief economist, Michael Mussa, that the U.S. stock market appeared high.
Mussa said Wednesday the market seemed to be on the "rich side," while also noting market fundamentals were "quite strong."

In its World Economic Outlook, the IMF said it saw the risk of a further big drop in stock prices in the United States and elsewhere, but suggested it would not be enough to help trigger an economic recession.

The IMF's rhetoric comes roughly four months after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan rocked global markets by suggesting stock prices might be too high as a result of "irrational exuberance" among investors.

Oppenheimer's Metz said he expected an orderly and restrained tempering of "equity mania" if the Federal Reserve moves, as the markets anticipate, to raise interest rates again in the months ahead. Last month the Fed raised short-term interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point in a bid to ward off inflationary pressures.
But Metz and other analysts noted that cautioning from IMF officials could help heighten awareness of the dangers posed by a soaring stock market.
"When markets move sharply in a volatile manner, sometimes it's best to temper them via jawboning and this appears to be such an attempt," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.

Ackerman was sanguine about what he termed a recent "shift to substance" in the market in which investors were focusing increasingly on value and less on momentum, but said some caution was appropriate.

"U.S. investors right now seem to be buying better quality stocks with a history of good management, growth and substance ... but we are looking at price-to-earnings ratios that may be a bit on the puffy side," Ackerman said.
The IMF's Mussa called the recent stock market bounceback "reassuring" and said it suggested the risks of a large downturn were probably not that great.
On Thursday afternoon, the Dow stood at roughly 6,810, almost 300 points lower than its recent peak of 7,085.
